1 Enoch (Ethiopian tradition) Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1-36) (c. 200 BC)

'The book of the words of righteousness, and of the reprimand of the eternal Watchers in accordance with the command of the Holy Great One in that vision' — the literary-canonical self-description of the section that follows. The text identifies itself as 'the book' (mäṣḥaf) of the words of righteousness — claiming for itself the canonical-scriptural status that the Tewahedo tradition recognizes. The naming of God as 'the Holy Great One' (Qadūs ʿAbiy) becomes a standard Tewahedo liturgical title, preserved in the Anaphora.

Enoch's ascent vision begins: 'I was borne aloft in the clouds, and they raised me upward... and the winds in the vision made me fly and lifted me upward.' This is the foundational Jewish-apocalyptic throne-vision pattern that Ezekiel's chariot, Daniel's Ancient of Days, and Revelation's heavenly throne room all develop. Enoch's vision precedes the prophetic and apocalyptic literature it patterns. The Tewahedo liturgical tradition draws explicit cross-reference between Enoch's ascent and the eucharistic anaphora's heavenly-court invocations: the worshipper at the altar is ushered into the same throne-room Enoch beheld.

candidates.draft_body:
1 Enoch (Ethiopian tradition) Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1-36) (c. 200 BC)

'And I beheld a lofty throne: its appearance was as crystal, and the wheels thereof as the shining sun, and there was the vision of cherubim. And from underneath the throne came streams of flaming fire so that I could not look thereon' — the central throne-vision of 1 Enoch's first half. The throne with wheels, crystal appearance, cherubim, and streaming fire combines Ezekiel 1's chariot, Daniel 7's Ancient of Days throne, and the Sinai theophany. Enoch's vision becomes the canonical Tewahedo template for every subsequent throne-vision in Christian apocalyptic literature, and the Mäṣḥafä Hēnok's liturgical reading on the Feast of the Transfiguration explicitly connects Enoch's beholding with Peter, James, and John's beholding on Tabor.

candidates.draft_body:
1 Enoch (Ethiopian tradition) Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1-36) (c. 200 BC)

Of the Most High in the throne vision: 'No angel could enter and could behold His face by reason of the magnificence and glory, and no flesh could behold Him' — the divine inaccessibility even to the highest angels. The 'no angel could enter' establishes the radical otherness of God even from the angelic order: God is not merely the highest among the heavenly hierarchy but qualitatively other than the entire creaturely order, including angels. This grounds the Tewahedo apophatic theological tradition: divine essence is incomprehensible to every creature, including the highest cherubim and seraphim.
